prompt_text:
A primary care research team collected routine screening data to study how systolic blood pressure varies with basic patient characteristics that are available at check-in. The original clinic extract contained 120 adult visits, but 24 records were not usable because at least one of the required fields was missing or the blood pressure reading failed the clinic’s quality check. The working file has 96 complete patient records.

For each patient, the recorded fields are age in years, body mass index in kg/m², current smoking status as yes or no, and seated systolic blood pressure in mmHg. Ages in the clinic sample are centered around middle adulthood, roughly 52 years on average with a broad spread of about 14 years. Body mass index values are mostly in the overweight range, averaging about 27.5 kg/m² with a spread of about 4.8 kg/m². About 22% of the patients are current smokers.

The systolic blood pressure measurements are all positive clinical readings and are recorded as continuous mmHg values. In the 96 usable records, the average systolic pressure is 103.56 mmHg, with a typical spread of 3.79 mmHg. The median is 103.68 mmHg. The middle half of patients fall from 100.60 to 106.12 mmHg, the 90th percentile is 109.19 mmHg, and the 99th percentile is 111.90 mmHg. The values are fairly concentrated, without obvious extreme high readings in this subset.

We know each patient’s age, body mass index, and smoking status at the visit. We do not know how much each of these factors contributes to the observed systolic pressure in this clinic population, or how large the remaining visit-to-visit and measurement differences are after accounting for those fields. The goal is to use these records to predict systolic blood pressure for a new patient record containing only age, body mass index, and smoking status.
